recognitions.title: This week, three separate claims of having fixed something didn't survive a single news cycle
recognitions.explanation: Across information warfare, foreign policy and debt management, the same pattern showed up: an announcement of control or resolution, followed within about a day by the other side, or the market, contradicting it. Iran claimed a sea mine sank a tanker in the Strait of Hormuz; the US called it a lie within the same cycle. A war-powers vote claimed to end a war it has no power to end. The Fed raised rates to signal it had inflation under control, and the bond market answered by pushing yields to an 18-year high. The pattern isn't that these claims are false when made - it's that none of them are built to survive contact with the next news cycle.

evidence.text: Iran's IRGC announced the tanker El Gaia hit a Hormuz sea mine - a claim of accident, not attack. Within the same news cycle, US CENTCOM called it "false," saying Iran itself struck the already-disabled ship again by drone. The claim didn't survive contact with the next report.

The House voted 220-204 for a third time to pass a war-powers resolution ending the Iran war - a real vote, a real majority, and it still changes nothing: the resolution won't reach Trump's desk, and he'd veto it if it did. Three votes, zero effect on the war itself.

The Fed hiked rates a quarter point Sept 16 - its first increase since 2023 - meant to signal control over inflation. Instead the 10-year Treasury yield jumped straight past 5%, its highest since 2007, as Chair Warsh flagged persistent inflation risk and one more hike this year.

recognitions.title: Three things that looked like resolutions this week all deferred the real question to later
recognitions.explanation: A ceasefire, a court ruling, and a shipping framework all landed this week wearing the shape of a resolution — and in each case, the people closest to it said out loud that the actual question is still open. A peace roadmap got its first verification mission, not a verified peace. A Supreme Court stay resolved a procedural fight while its own justices noted the underlying legality is untouched. A transit deal is 'in principle' and 'still being finalized.' Each is a real step. None of them is the thing a headline would make it sound like.

evidence.text: M23 declared DRC's Ebola outbreak over in its territory in late June. As of Sept 16, cases keep climbing nationally (7,404 confirmed, 3,577 dead) - Ituri cooling as promised, but North Kivu rising fast enough that its treatment facilities are nearing full capacity.

María Corina Machado backs a long-term US role in Venezuelan oil but is now the one publicly asking who actually signed the 100-year deal, who finances it, and how Venezuelans benefit - the same basic questions a genuine resolution would already have answered.

SCOTUS blocked Trump's mail-ballot restrictions for the midterms - a resolution in form. But Kavanaugh's concurrence conceded the rule might be legal, just too late to implement fairly this cycle, and commentators call the ruling "cryptic," not the Court's last word on the underlying question.

The postponed Hormuz meeting wasn't even a negotiation to begin with - Gulf states were only ever going to be briefed on a Tehran-Muscat deal already finalized behind closed doors. And the delay wasn't Iran's or Oman's call: Saudi Arabia requested it, over an unrelated grievance about Houthi attacks on its own territory.
